title: Zephyrine and the Uniform
premise: In 1918, Quentin Sandoval drives for suffragist Zephyrine Marchand and quietly reads every letter she dictates, believing history belongs to other people. When occupying soldiers requisition the town and seize the ledger holding the names of every woman who petitioned, marched, or sheltered deserters, Quentin realizes invisibility was always a fiction someone else wrote. To save Zephyrine from a tribunal, Quentin must smuggle the true record — testimony, letters, names — past censors and into the hands of an armistice commission before the victors' historians write the town out of existence. The book ends with the armistice signed and the ledger partially restored: justice arrives late, incomplete, and only because ordinary people refused to let the record be written without them.
about_author: Sebastian Dunmore is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing confiscated municipal records from occupied French towns. They write historical fiction about the paperwork of survival — the ledgers, letters, and lists that decide who gets remembered.

chapters.title: The Man Who Reads Other People's Mail
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Establishes their routine: driving Zephyrine to suffrage meetings, secretly reading her dictated letters in the garage at night. Emotional beat: comfortable self-deception — Quentin believes being a witness to history means never appearing in it.

chapters.title: Zephyrine's Ledger
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Zephyrine keeps a ledger of names — petitioners, marchers, women who hid a deserter son. She catches Quentin reading it and, instead of anger, makes them her second pair of eyes. Beat: reluctant trust; Quentin begins to matter.

chapters.title: Grey Trucks on the Market Road
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Army trucks arrive unannounced; officers requisition the town hall, billets, horses, and Quentin's motorcar for 'administrative use.' Beat: dread arriving as bureaucracy — polite forms that erase everything.

chapters.title: Requisition Notice No. 44
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with a young clerk, Lieutenant Aubry, who genuinely believes in orderly process. The ledger is seized as 'subversive documentation.' Beat: the horror of procedure; both characters feel the trap closing politely.

chapters.title: What the Names Weigh
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. She recounts why each name is in the ledger — including one that would hang a family if read aloud. Beat: grief converted to purpose; she refuses to flee, insisting records can be rebuilt from memory.

chapters.title: A Driver's Useful Invisibility
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Officers treat Quentin as furniture, discussing tribunal schedules within earshot. Quentin starts memorizing dates and names. Beat: the first thrill of agency — invisibility becomes a tool instead of a shield.

chapters.title: Letters Through the Censor's Hands
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin volunteers to run mail for the garrison, reading everything en route, copying fragments onto cigarette papers. Beat: complicity and craft; the reader becomes the writer of the hidden record.

chapters.title: Lieutenant Aubry's Doubt
chapters.summary: Aubry's POV. Ordered to falsify the requisition inventory to hide a soldier's death during a raid, he hesitates. Beat: conscience cracking under career pressure; he notices Quentin watching him.

chapters.title: The Widow Perrin Testifies
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. She takes secret testimony from Widow Perrin, whose son was shot as a deserter after sheltering by the town. Beat: testimony as sacrament; the spoken truth enters the hidden ledger.

chapters.title: Checkpoint at the Mill Bridge
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A copied page is nearly discovered during a search; Quentin swallows it, literally. Beat: terror and dark comedy; the price of survival becomes physical.

chapters.title: An Offer Written in Pencil
chapters.summary: Aubry's POV. Aubry privately offers Quentin blank requisition forms in exchange for nothing he can name yet. Beat: uneasy alliance between two people using the system against itself.

chapters.title: The Tribunal List
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin copies the tribunal docket: Zephyrine will be tried for sedition the week before the armistice. Beat: clock starts ticking; personal stakes fuse with the historical deadline.

chapters.title: What Zephyrine Refuses to Burn
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Advised to destroy all papers, she instead has Quentin photograph nothing and memorize everything — 'paper burns; memory needs killing.' Beat: mentorship completing itself; Quentin becomes the archive.

chapters.title: The Armistice Rumor
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, mostly Quentin's POV. News of negotiations splits the town: some want revenge now, others silence forever. Beat: community fracturing; justice outside the law looks like mob law too.

chapters.title: Aubry's Choice
chapters.summary: Aubry's POV. His superior orders him to certify the falsified inventory; instead he seals the true one and passes it to Quentin. Beat: sacrifice without heroics — he knows it ends his career, maybe his life.

chapters.title: The Night Drive
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin drives the sealed record through checkpoints toward the armistice commission's forward office, using forged requisition stamps. Beat: sustained suspense; the invisible man finally visible in headlights.

chapters.title: Interrogation in the Town Hall
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Arrested early, she turns her hearing into testimony, speaking names into the official transcript. Beat: defiant climax of voice — the courtroom becomes her printing press.

chapters.title: The Commission Clerk
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. At the commission office, a weary clerk must decide whether the sealed record is admissible before the armistice signing. Beat: quiet climax — one tired stranger holds the whole book in his hands.

chapters.title: Signed at the Eleventh Hour
chapters.summary: Split POV. The armistice is signed; the commission accepts the record minutes before sealing its archives; Zephyrine's tribunal is dissolved as jurisdiction evaporates. Beat: relief shadowed by arbitrariness — survival by inches and clerks.

chapters.title: What the Victors Print
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Weeks later, official histories omit the occupation entirely. Zephyrine's restored ledger circulates hand-to-hand. Beat: sobering — the record exists but not in the places power reads.

chapters.title: The Second Pair of Eyes
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. She formally names Quentin co-keeper of the ledger, no longer driver or reader but author. Beat: identity claimed; Quentin stops being furniture in anyone's story.

chapters.title: Every Letter, Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, years later. An aged Quentin reads the ledger aloud at the town's memorial, adding names the victors' historians never printed. Final beat: history happens to everyone; the only question is who writes it down.
